title: Interpretations: Copenhagen, Many-Worlds, Pilot Wave and More

cards.b: Everyone agrees how to calculate with quantum theory. Almost nobody agrees what it says about reality. The disagreements are called interpretations. Be careful: most make the same predictions, so experiments cannot yet choose between them. Treat each as a story told about the same equations.

Quantum theory has two rules: smooth evolution of ψ (Schrödinger) and a random jump at measurement (Born). What counts as a "measurement"? Why do we see only one result? Where does the quantum world end and the everyday world begin? Each interpretation answers differently.

cards.h: Bohr, Heisenberg, and "shut up and calculate"
cards.b: Developed around Niels Bohr and Werner Heisenberg, and aired at the 1927 Solvay conference. Core idea: ψ is a tool for predicting results; measurement results are what is real; do not ask what happens in between. Several versions exist, so "the Copenhagen interpretation" is loose. It treats collapse as basic and leaves the measuring apparatus unexplained. "Shut up and calculate" is a joking summary of the practical attitude.

Hugh Everett III proposed there is no collapse. ψ always evolves smoothly; when a measurement happens, the observer becomes entangled and all outcomes occur, each in its own branch. We only experience one branch at a time. Strength: simplest equations. Cost: a vast number of unseen branches, and a puzzle over what "odds" mean when everything happens.

Louis de Broglie suggested it in 1927; David Bohm revived it in 1952. A particle has a definite position at all times and is steered by the wavefunction. It reproduces all standard predictions, and the "randomness" comes from not knowing the starting position. Cost: it is explicitly non-local (distant parts instantly guide each other), which Bell's theorem allows but which clashes with relativity's spirit.

• Collapse models (GRW, 1986; Penrose): collapse is a real physical process, rare for single particles and quick for big objects. These predict small differences and are testable; so far experiments have ruled out some versions.
  • QBism (Fuchs): ψ is an agent's personal degree of belief.
  • Relational QM (Rovelli, 1996): properties exist only relative to other systems.
  • Consistent histories and superdeterminism.

Bell tests rule out local hidden-variable theories, so every interpretation must be non-local, deny single outcomes, or deny free choice. Beyond that, the mainstream ones agree. In informal polls, no view has a majority. In a 2013 poll of about 30 specialists, Copenhagen led with about 40% (Schlosshauer, Kofler and Zeilinger). Collapse models are the first group to predict something different, and labs are testing them.

• "Many-worlds lets you travel between universes." Branches never communicate.
  • "Consciousness causes collapse is mainstream." It is a rare minority view (von Neumann and Wigner raised it).
  • "Experiments have proved Copenhagen." They have not chosen any.

E.C.G. Sudarshan, one of India's most famous theorists, helped build the language used to describe measurement and decoherence in open quantum systems (GKSL equation, 1976, with Gorini, Kossakowski and Lindblad). The ancient "many ways of seeing" tradition in Indian philosophy is sometimes compared with interpretations, but those are analogies, not physics.

• All interpretations agree on predictions but tell different stories.
  • Copenhagen (collapse), many-worlds (branches), pilot wave (particles plus guide), collapse models (testable).
  • Bell tests narrow the choices but do not pick one.

Think about it

  1. Which interpretations keep a single definite world, and what do they give up?
  2. Why are collapse models more scientific in the sense of testing than others?
